candidate_relations.label: Lupus vulgaris
candidate_relations.reason: Lupus vulgaris is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and presents with different histopathology (tuberculoid granulomas, no grenz zone, no foamy histiocytes in storiform pattern). The clinical record shows acid-fast bacilli within foamy histiocytes in a storiform pattern with a grenz zone and high bacterial index, all hallmarks of leprosy, not cutaneous TB.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Lupus vulgaris is cutaneous tuberculosis, not leprosy

candidate_relations.label: Lupus erythematosus
candidate_relations.reason: While the patient has positive ANA, anti-Ro52, and anti-cardiolipin antibodies that could suggest lupus erythematosus, the histopathology with abundant acid-fast bacilli within foamy histiocytes, storiform pattern, grenz zone, and high bacterial index (4.8) definitively points to leprosy. The autoantibodies are known to occur as reactive phenomena in lepromatous/histoid leprosy.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Positive ANA and anti-Ro52 are present but LE is not the final diagnosis

candidate_relations.label: Lepromatous leprosy
candidate_relations.reason: Histoid leprosy is a distinct variant of lepromatous leprosy characterized by discrete firm nodules, spindle-shaped foamy histiocytes arranged in a storiform pattern, and very high bacterial index — all present here. Lepromatous leprosy is the parent diagnosis but lacks the required specificity of the histoid subtype, which is the benchmark reference.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Lepromatous leprosy is the parent category; histoid leprosy is a specific subtype requiring additional morphological criteria

case_quality_flags: Autoantibody positivity (ANA, anti-Ro52, anti-cardiolipin, elevated RF) may represent reactive immunological phenomena in lepromatous/histoid leprosy rather than a co-existing autoimmune disease
Childhood exposure history (neighbor visits ages 3-18) supports long incubation period consistent with M. leprae infection
